passage:
You want to know how it felt, Bhupen, getting the rank? Okay. Honestly.
I'm Aditi. From Class 8, Papa had a number stuck on the fridge: “Top 500.” Every uncle at every wedding asked about it. My best friend's brother got top 300, so the target became mine too.
I studied for four years. I skipped my cousin's wedding. I stopped painting completely.
The day the result came, rank 412, everyone was crying and clapping. Papa called forty people. I sat on the bathroom floor and waited to feel happy.
It didn't come. Not that day, not that week. It felt like I'd run a race someone else had entered me in.
Now I'm in a good college, and I'm fine. But the only time I've felt that deep, quiet contentment this year was painting the hostel mural last month. Nobody asked me to do that.

qa.q: What rank did Aditi get?
qa.a: Aditi got rank 412.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel on the bathroom floor on result day?
qa.a: Aditi felt empty and hollow, waiting for happiness that never came because the goal had been Papa's and the uncles', not Aditi's own.

qa.q: What could Aditi do now to find more satisfaction?
qa.a: Aditi could make regular space for painting and think about which goals truly match Aditi's own values.

qa.q: How might Papa see result day differently from Aditi?
qa.a: Papa probably felt thrilled and proud, calling forty people, without knowing Aditi felt nothing.

grounding: The monologue shows a young adult reaching a rank target set by family and feeling empty, because the goal did not match personal values.

passage:
January: Kavitha's older brother Suraj said a bank job was the safest life. “Clear the exam, and you're set.” So Kavitha studied for it every night after college, though her notebook margins filled with sketches of buildings.
August: The result came. She had cleared it. Suraj hugged her; Amma distributed sweets to the whole street. Kavitha smiled for the photos. Inside, she felt flat, as if she'd crossed someone else's finish line.
October: On her first week of training, she sat at a counter stamping forms. At lunch she walked past a new library being built next door and stood watching the architects argue over a drawing for twenty minutes.
That night she wrote in her notebook: “I got what Suraj wanted for me. I don't know yet what I want. But it's not this.”

qa.q: What did Kavitha's notebook margins fill with?
qa.a: They filled with sketches of buildings.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel when the result came, even though she had cleared it?
qa.a: She felt flat and empty, as if she had crossed someone else's finish line.

qa.q: What could Kavitha do next?
qa.a: She could explore her interest in buildings, perhaps by talking to an architect or a career counsellor, before deciding her next step.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel if he read the notebook entry?
qa.a: Suraj might feel hurt or confused, having truly believed the bank job was best for her.

grounding: The three beats show a young adult reaching a goal set by her brother and feeling empty because it did not match her own values.

passage:
Ankita, you're asking if you should do the MBA just because everyone in your batch is. Let me, your Kalyani Mashi, tell you about 1994.
I was twenty-one. My father had decided I would be a chartered accountant, like him. I passed every exam, first attempt. The day I got my final result, the whole family came to our flat in Kolkata. My father gave a speech.
I remember standing in the kitchen, holding a plate of sandesh, feeling nothing. Nothing at all. I kept thinking, Is this it?
I worked as an accountant for six years before I let myself admit I wanted to teach. When I finally did, the first day in a classroom, I felt more alive than on that whole result day.
Don't chase a finish line someone else drew for you.

qa.q: What did Kalyani hold in the kitchen on result day?
qa.a: She held a plate of sandesh.

qa.q: Why did young Kalyani feel nothing on result day?
qa.a: She felt empty because the goal had been her father's; passing it gave no real satisfaction to her own values.

qa.q: At what point in the story did Kalyani's path change?
qa.a: After six years as an accountant, when she let herself admit she wanted to teach and started in a classroom.

qa.q: How might Kalyani's father have felt on the result day?
qa.a: He likely felt proud and happy, giving a speech, without noticing his daughter felt empty.

grounding: The elder's memory shows a young woman reaching a career goal her father set and feeling empty, since it did not match her values.

passage:
Noor's big aim for the year was a half marathon in December. She broke it into monthly steps: run 5 km by March, 10 km by June, 15 km by October. Each week, three runs. Every Sunday, she and her flatmate Mohit had tea and reviewed the week.
Then July came. Mumbai flooded. The park was underwater, her mother fell ill, and for three weeks Noor didn't run at all.
The old Noor would have thrown the plan away. Instead, at Sunday tea, she said, “I missed three weeks.”
Mohit said, “You also looked after your mother. What can you do this week?”
“Stair climbing in the building. Twenty minutes, three times.”
“Good.”
She pushed the 15 km target from October to November and moved the race goal to the January one. The plan bent. It didn't break.

qa.q: What was Noor's big aim for the year?
qa.a: Her aim was to run a half marathon in December.

qa.q: How did Noor feel when she admitted missing three weeks?
qa.a: She seemed disappointed but calm, able to admit it without giving up because the weekly review was kind.

qa.q: Why did Noor's plan survive the floods and her mother's illness?
qa.a: Because she reviewed it kindly every week and adjusted it, switching to stair climbing and moving targets instead of abandoning the goal.

qa.q: How does Mohit see the missed weeks?
qa.a: Mohit sees them as a real-life interruption, noting she also cared for her mother, rather than as failure.

grounding: The passage shows an adult splitting a big aim into monthly and weekly steps and reviewing it kindly, so the plan bends with real life.

passage:
Trisha wanted to clear her company-secretary finals by next December. On New Year's Day in her Kolkata flat, she wrote it at the top of a sheet of paper.
Underneath: January–March, module one. April–June, module two. And under that, each week: three chapters, one mock test.
Every Sunday evening, she and her friend Francis video-called for twenty minutes. He was learning the guitar and had his own plan. They each asked the same two questions: What did you do? What gets in the way this week?
In May she had a work audit and managed only one chapter a week. She felt a flash of panic. Francis said, “So adjust. What's realistic for May?”
She moved two chapters into June. She didn't call herself lazy. By September she was only two weeks behind, and still going.

qa.q: How long were Trisha and Francis's Sunday calls?
qa.a: They were twenty minutes long.

qa.q: What did Trisha feel when the audit slowed her down in May?
qa.a: She felt a flash of panic, but then steadied as she adjusted the plan instead of blaming herself.

qa.q: What made Trisha's approach work?
qa.a: A big aim linked to monthly and weekly steps, with a kind weekly review that let her adjust when real life got in the way.

qa.q: How might Francis benefit from the Sunday calls too?
qa.a: Francis also gets support for his guitar plan and probably feels encouraged by sharing the routine.

grounding: The passage shows an adult splitting a big exam goal into monthly and weekly steps with a kind weekly review, keeping the plan flexible.

“Speak basic Kannada by next year, so I can talk to patients on my ward without a translator,” said Sarika.
“And this month?”
“Hospital phrases. Pain, breathing, food.”
“This week?”
“Ten phrases. Practise with the ward aunties at lunch.”
“How did it go?”
Sarika sighed. “I did six. Night shifts all week. I was so tired.”
“Six is more than zero.”
“It's not ten.”
“It's not ten,” Leela agreed. “So what's next week? Ten again, or six?”
Sarika thought. “Eight. And I'll do them on the bus.”
“Deal. Also, you asked a patient if she was hungry, in Kannada. You told me on Tuesday.”
Sarika smiled. “She laughed at my accent. But she answered.”

passage:
In the one-room school at Palasgaon, the teacher had put out new jigsaw puzzles donated by the block office. Everyone rushed to the boxes.
Tushar, nine, took the old bullock-cart puzzle again. He had done it perhaps twenty times. He knew every piece.
His older sister Chandrika, helping the teacher, knelt beside him. “Try the new one with the train. It has more pieces.”
“No. This one.”
“You'll get the hang of it.”
“What if I can't do it? Everyone will see.” He clutched the bullock-cart box.
He finished it in six minutes, as usual, and felt safe. At the next mat, Rukhsar was struggling with the train, laughing when pieces didn't fit, and slowly getting it.
Tushar watched her. He wanted to try. He didn't.

qa.q: How many times had Tushar done the bullock-cart puzzle?
qa.a: He had done it perhaps twenty times.

qa.q: Why did Tushar keep choosing the old puzzle?
qa.a: He was afraid of being wrong in front of everyone, so the familiar puzzle felt safe.

qa.q: How could Chandrika help Tushar try the new puzzle?
qa.a: She could sit with him and start it together, making mistakes feel normal and fun.

qa.q: How does Rukhsar's approach differ from Tushar's?
qa.a: Rukhsar laughs at pieces that don't fit and keeps going, so she is learning while Tushar stays safe but stuck.

grounding: The passage shows a child who fears being wrong choosing only a puzzle he already knows, which feels safe but blocks learning.

passage:
At the maths club in Accra, the teacher put out a stack of new logic puzzles. Kwame picked the grid puzzle he'd already solved last week.
“That one again?” his friend Jamal asked.
“I like it.”
“You could try the pyramid one. It's hard. Nobody's done it.”
Kwame shook his head quickly. What if he got it wrong? What if everyone saw him stuck?
He filled in the grid he already knew, fast and neat, and felt calm.
Jamal took the pyramid puzzle and got it wrong three times. He groaned, laughed, rubbed out his answers, and tried a new idea. On the fourth try he got it and did a little dance.
Kwame looked at his neat, finished grid. It had been easy. He hadn't learned anything new today, and he knew it.

qa.q: How many times did Jamal get the pyramid puzzle wrong?
qa.a: He got it wrong three times before solving it on the fourth try.

qa.q: Why did Kwame shake his head at the pyramid puzzle?
qa.a: He was afraid of getting it wrong and being seen stuck, so the known grid felt safer.

qa.q: What could the teacher do to help Kwame try harder puzzles?
qa.a: The teacher could praise trying and mistakes, or pair Kwame with Jamal so being stuck feels shared and normal.

qa.q: How does Jamal experience getting it wrong?
qa.a: Jamal treats mistakes as part of the game, groaning and laughing, and feels delighted when he finally solves it.

grounding: The passage shows a child who fears being wrong repeating a puzzle he already knows, which feels safe but stops him learning.

passage:
At the Saturday puzzle corner of the Guwahati community library, Lavanya, ten, always chose the same easy sudoku book, with answers she half-remembered.
The librarian, Himani Baideu, held out a new book. “Killer sudoku. It's like a riddle. Want to try?”
Lavanya's face tightened. “I don't know those.”
“That's the point. You'd learn.”
“But I might get it wrong.” She said it in a whisper, as if wrong were a dangerous word.
Himani sat down beside her. “I'll do the first one with you. We'll both get it wrong a bit.”
Lavanya hesitated, then shook her head and opened the easy book. She filled in the first grid, fast and perfectly, and let out a breath. Himani left the new book on the table, just in case.

qa.q: What did Himani Baideu offer Lavanya?
qa.a: She offered a new killer sudoku book.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya whisper that she might get it wrong?
qa.a: She is afraid of being wrong, so the familiar easy book feels safe and comforting.

qa.q: What did Himani do that might help next time?
qa.a: She offered to try it together and admitted they'd both get it wrong a bit, and left the new book nearby as a quiet invitation.

qa.q: What might Himani be thinking when she leaves the new book on the table?
qa.a: Himani is probably hopeful and patient, trusting that Lavanya may feel ready another day.

grounding: The passage shows a child who fears being wrong sticking to puzzles she already knows, which feels safe but blocks new learning.

passage:
The notice for the inter-school debate went up on the Monday after Charu's loss. Her name wasn't on the sign-up sheet.
Her teammate Chaitanya found her in the library. “You're not signing up?”
“No point.”
“You were brilliant in the last round.”
“I lost, Chaitanya. In front of the whole auditorium. My rebuttal fell apart and the other team laughed.” She stared at her book. “I'm obviously not a debater.”
“You lost one debate.”
“It's not about one debate. It's about what it says. That I'm the girl who froze.”
Chaitanya sat down. “Nobody remembers you froze. They remember your opening.”
Charu shook her head. She'd rehearsed in her mind how it would feel to lose again, and it felt unbearable. The sheet closed on Friday. Her name still wasn't there.

qa.q: When did the sign-up sheet close?
qa.a: The sheet closed on Friday.

qa.q: Why did Charu refuse to sign up for the next debate?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and afraid, believing the loss showed she was “the girl who froze,” so losing again felt unbearable.

qa.q: What could help Charu separate the loss from her worth?
qa.a: Talking with a coach about what went wrong in the rebuttal and practising it, so the loss becomes a skill to fix rather than a verdict on her.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya see Charu's loss?
qa.a: Chaitanya sees it as one debate and remembers her strong opening, not a sign she isn't a debater.

grounding: The passage shows a teenager who lost a debate feeling her worth has dropped and avoiding the next contest out of fear of what failure says about her.

passage:
Subject: Taking my name off

Dear Himani Ma'am,

I'm writing to take my name off the district debate list. I know you put me on it because you think I can do it. I'm sorry.

After last month's final, I don't think I should represent the school again. I lost the vote badly. I forgot my second point halfway through. Everyone could see.

It's not the topic. I actually like the topic. It's that I keep thinking, if I lose again, it will prove what everyone must be thinking: that I got lucky before, and I'm not actually good.

I'd rather not debate than find that out in front of everyone.

Please give my place to someone who deserves it.

Anjali

passage:
You're asking why I'm not in the quiz team this year, Vinita. Okay, fine.
I'm Baljeet. Last year, at the state quiz final, I buzzed early on the last question. I said “Mars” and the answer was “Venus.” We lost by five points. The whole team had to walk off stage past everyone.
Nobody blamed me out loud. That was almost worse. On the bus back, I just kept thinking: you're the one who ruined it. You're not actually smart. You just looked smart.
So when the sign-up came this year, I didn't go. I told everyone I was busy. The truth is I'm scared. Not of the questions. I know tons. I'm scared of what it would mean if I messed up again. Like it would prove I'm the person who loses.

passage:
Kavitha, you're asking whether to take the easier elective to keep your score up. Let me, your Gautam Mama, tell you what I did at nineteen.
In Pune, in second year, we could pick one elective. There was astronomy, which I'd loved since I was a boy on the terrace with a borrowed telescope. And there was business communication, which everyone said was an easy A.
I told myself it was about my scholarship. It wasn't, really. I was scared. What if I loved astronomy and wasn't good at it? My marks would drop and so would everyone's opinion of me.
I took business communication. I got my A.
Forty years later, I still have the telescope. I still wonder. That grade didn't matter to anyone after a year. The fear chose for me, and I let it.

qa.q: Which elective did young Gautam choose?
qa.a: Young Gautam chose business communication, which everyone said was an easy A.

qa.q: Why did young Gautam really choose the easy elective?
qa.a: He was afraid of loving astronomy and not being good at it, which would drop his marks and others' opinion of him.

qa.q: At what point in the story could Gautam have chosen differently?
qa.a: At the elective choice in second year, he could have taken astronomy and accepted some risk to his marks.

qa.q: How might the friends who called it an easy A have seen Gautam's choice?
qa.a: They probably saw it as a sensible, smart move, not realising fear was behind it.

grounding: The uncle's memory shows a student choosing an easy elective to protect his grades and never trying the field he loved.

passage:
The elective registration portal closed at 5 p.m., and at 4:15 it kept crashing. Ojas sat in the college cyber café with his cousin Aadhya, refreshing again and again.
Two options: “Film-making workshop: portfolio-based grading” or “Office tools: guaranteed high scores.”
Ojas had spent every holiday since Class 8 making short films on his phone.
“So, film-making, obviously?” Aadhya said.
“My CGPA is 9.2. If the portfolio's bad, I could get a C.”
“Could.”
“And then the placement cutoff…” He trailed off. The page loaded for a second. His finger hovered over film-making, then clicked office tools.
Submitted: 4:52.
“You look like you just lost something,” Aadhya said quietly.
Ojas closed the laptop. “I kept my 9.2.”

qa.q: What was Ojas's CGPA?
qa.a: His CGPA was 9.2.

qa.q: Why did Ojas click office tools instead of film-making?
qa.a: He was afraid a bad portfolio would lower his grade and hurt his placement chances, so the safe option felt necessary.

qa.q: What could Ojas try to keep his love of film alive?
qa.a: He could join a film club or make films outside class, or talk to the film teacher about how grading works before deciding next time.

qa.q: How does Aadhya see his choice?
qa.a: Aadhya sees that he gave up something he loves, saying he looks like he just lost something.

grounding: The passage shows a student under time pressure choosing the safe, easy course to protect his grades and giving up the field he loves.

passage:
Shankar had played the sitar since he was seven. At his college in Hyderabad, there was a music composition minor, and it was all he could talk about for a month.
Then he looked at the grading: original compositions, public performance, strict jury. He looked at his 9.5 GPA.
His sister Nirmala found him with two forms. “Music composition or accounting basics?”
“Accounting,” he said.
“You hate accounting.”
“It's an easy ten. Composition could drag me down. And what if I'm not as good as I think? Then what?”
“Then you'd find out, and learn.”
“Or find out I'm average.” He signed the accounting form.
That evening, he played the sitar in his room for two hours. Nirmala listened from the corridor and didn't say anything.

qa.a: He had played the sitar since he was seven.

qa.q: Why did Shankar sign the accounting form?

qa.a: Nirmala probably feels sad and worried, sensing he gave up something he loves.

passage:
March: Charu's café in Bhopal closed after eleven months. She sat among the stacked chairs, feeling crushed. Then she opened a notebook and wrote: What went wrong? Wrong location, rent too high for the footfall. Menu too big. I did everything myself and burnt out.
April: She told three people she trusted: her mentor, her aunt, and her friend Yusuf. Yusuf listened and asked, “Which of these would you fix first?” She said, “Menu. And I'd start smaller.”
November: Charu started a tiffin service from her home kitchen: five dishes only, delivery to two office buildings, one helper from the start. On her notebook's first page, she stuck the April list. When orders dropped in the rain, she checked the list, adjusted and kept going. It was hard. But it wasn't a verdict anymore. It was data.

qa.q: How long had Charu's café been open before it closed?
qa.a: It had been open for eleven months.

qa.q: How did Charu feel among the stacked chairs, and what did she do?
qa.a: She felt crushed, but she opened a notebook and wrote what went wrong, turning the pain into lessons.

qa.q: What did Charu apply to her next venture?
qa.a: A small menu of five dishes, starting smaller, and a helper from the start, using the lessons from the café.

qa.q: How might Yusuf see Charu's failure?
qa.a: Yusuf treats it as something to learn from, asking which problem she would fix first rather than judging her.

grounding: The three beats show an adult writing lessons from a failed café, sharing them with trusted people, and applying them to the next venture.

passage:
Indu, you're sad your bakery idea didn't work. Let me, your Minakshi Periamma, tell you about my tailoring shop.
I was twenty-five. I opened a little shop in Madurai with my savings, and in one year I had to close it. I cried for a week. I thought, That's it, I'm not a business person.
Then my own mother said, “Write down what happened. Not what you are. What happened.”
So I wrote: Too many designs. No regular customers. Shop too far from the bus stand.
I told my mother and two friends. They added things I hadn't seen.
Three years later I started again, from home, only blouses, near the school. I kept that list in the drawer. That business fed our family for thirty years.

qa.a: Her mother likely felt proud and relieved to see her daughter use the failure to build something lasting.

passage:
Shreya's online plant shop had shut down in August after eight months. She had very little money left, and the rain was coming down the day she set up at the Sunday market under a borrowed tarpaulin.
Before, she'd sat at her kitchen table and written: What did I learn? Plants died in courier boxes. Too many varieties. Posting everywhere, selling nowhere.
She had shown the list to her sister Ritu and an old manager. Ritu had said, “So sell in person. Only hardy plants. Start small.”
Now, eight pots of money plants and snake plants, on one table, in the rain. A woman stopped, then another. By noon, six pots were gone.
Shreya wrote two new lines in the notebook under the tarpaulin: Rain brings fewer people but serious buyers. Need a sign with prices.

passage:
In the village school at Bishnupur, Darshan Sir asked, “Which is heavier, a kilo of cotton or a kilo of iron?”
Anirban's hand shot up. “Iron, Sir!” Then he saw Sir's eyebrow rise slightly.
“Um, no, cotton?” He watched Sir's face. Sir's mouth twitched. “No, the same! They're the same.”
“And why?”
Anirban didn't know why. He had only followed the eyebrow. His ears went hot.
Later, in the maths period, Sir asked what 7 times 8 was. Anirban knew it: 56. But before he answered, he glanced at Sir's face first, just to check.
“Anirban,” said Sir gently, “you don't need to read my face. Tell me what you think. Even if it's wrong.”

qa.q: What was Darshan Sir's first question?
qa.a: “Which is heavier, a kilo of cotton or a kilo of iron?”

qa.q: Why did Anirban keep changing his answer?
qa.a: He was anxious to please Sir, so he followed Sir's eyebrow and mouth instead of his own thinking.

qa.q: What did Darshan Sir say that could help Anirban think for himself?
qa.a: He told Anirban he doesn't need to read Sir's face and should say what he thinks, even if it's wrong.

qa.q: How might Darshan Sir feel watching Anirban glance at his face before 7 times 8?
qa.a: Sir probably feels concerned, realising the boy cares more about approval than his own answer.

grounding: The passage shows a child changing answers to match the teacher's face, with approval crowding out honest thought.

passage:
In Ms Noa's science class in Singapore, the question on the board was: “Why do puddles disappear on sunny days?”
Wei raised his hand. “The water sinks into the ground?”
Ms Noa tilted her head, just slightly.
“I mean, it goes up? Into the air?”
She smiled.
“Evaporation!” Wei said quickly, relieved. He had heard the word before. He didn't really know what it meant.
Later, when they did a worksheet, Wei kept looking up at Ms Noa's face every time she walked past his desk. If she slowed down, he rubbed out his answer. If she nodded, he kept it. By the end, half his sheet was rubbed thin.
When Ms Noa collected it, she noticed. “Wei, lots of rubbing. What was your first answer here?”
He blinked. He couldn't remember.

qa.q: What question was on the board?
qa.a: “Why do puddles disappear on sunny days?”

qa.q: Why did Wei rub out answers when Ms Noa slowed down?
qa.a: He was anxious for her approval and read her pace as a sign he was wrong, so her face mattered more than his own thinking.

qa.q: What could Ms Noa try to help Wei trust his own ideas?
qa.a: She could ask him to explain his first answer before she reacts, and praise his reasoning even when it's not correct.

passage:
At the Saturday drawing class in the community hall, Reena Ma'am asked the children to draw “what the rain feels like.”
Aparna, eight, started with grey lines. Reena Ma'am walked past and said nothing. Aparna stopped. Did no word mean bad?
She rubbed out the grey. She peeked at the girl beside her, whose paper got a “lovely!” from Ma'am. That girl had drawn rainbow umbrellas.
Aparna drew rainbow umbrellas.
When Ma'am came back, Aparna looked up at her face, waiting.
“Nice umbrellas,” Reena Ma'am said. “But I saw grey lines before. What were they?”
Aparna whispered, “How rain feels when I'm sad.”
Reena Ma'am crouched down. “That's a real answer. I'd love to see that one.”

qa.q: What did the girl beside Aparna draw?
qa.a: She drew rainbow umbrellas.

qa.q: Why did Aparna rub out her grey lines?
qa.a: She felt anxious when Reena Ma'am said nothing, fearing it meant disapproval, so she copied what seemed to please the teacher.

qa.q: What did Reena Ma'am do that could help Aparna think honestly?
qa.a: She asked about the grey lines and valued Aparna's real answer, showing honest ideas matter more than pleasing her.

qa.q: How might Reena Ma'am see Aparna's switch to rainbow umbrellas?
qa.a: Reena Ma'am may feel concerned that Aparna is drawing to please her, and curious about the grey lines, which looked more honest.

grounding: The passage shows a child changing her drawing to what seems to please the teacher, and approval crowding out honest expression.

passage:
Vandana, you told me you laughed at the joke about the new girl even though it made you feel sick. Let me, your Alka Maasi, tell you about me at fifteen.
In Jaipur, there was a group of girls I badly wanted to belong to. When they said a film was stupid, I said it was stupid, though I had loved it. When they made fun of a girl's oiled plait, I laughed loudest.
One night I went home and cried, because that girl was my neighbour, and she used to share her mangoes with me.
The next day I didn't laugh. I just stayed quiet. The group noticed. It was frightening. For a week I thought they'd drop me.
They didn't, not completely. And I got a little bit of myself back.

qa.q: What did the group make fun of?
qa.a: They made fun of a girl's oiled plait.

qa.q: Why did young Alka laugh loudest at the joke?
qa.a: She was afraid of being rejected by the group, so their approval mattered more to her than her own feelings.

qa.q: At what point in the story did Alka make a different choice?
qa.a: The next day, when she stayed quiet instead of laughing, risking the group's approval.

qa.q: How might the neighbour girl have felt hearing Alka laugh?
qa.a: The neighbour probably felt hurt and betrayed, since Alka was someone she shared mangoes with.

grounding: The aunt's memory shows a teenager agreeing with friends and laughing at jokes she disliked because the group's approval felt more important than herself.

passage:
The school trip bus to Mahabaleshwar was stuck in a four-hour traffic jam, and the back seats had turned into a stage. Damini, the loudest in their group, was rating everyone's outfits out of ten.
“Chetan, agree, na? Priyanka's jacket is a disaster.”
Chetan actually liked the jacket. It was the same colour as his mother's favourite shawl. “Total disaster,” he said, and everyone laughed.
Damini did a mocking voice of a teacher. Chetan thought it was mean. He laughed anyway, a beat too late.
By the third hour, his jaw ached from fake smiling. Priyanka was sitting two seats ahead, very still, earphones in but no music playing.
Chetan looked out at the fog. He had agreed with everything for three hours. He wasn't sure what he actually thought about anything anymore.

qa.q: How long was the traffic jam?
qa.a: It was a four-hour traffic jam.

qa.q: Why did Chetan call the jacket a disaster when he liked it?
qa.a: He was afraid of being left out of Damini's group, so their approval felt more important than his own view.

qa.q: What could Chetan try the next time Damini starts rating people?
qa.a: He could stay quiet or say something simple like “I like it, actually,” keeping some of his own view without starting a fight.

qa.q: What might it be like for Priyanka sitting two seats ahead?
qa.a: Priyanka probably feels humiliated and hurt, pretending to listen to music so no one sees her upset.

grounding: The passage shows a teenager on a long, stuck bus agreeing with friends and laughing at jokes he dislikes because the group's approval feels more important.

passage:
After the interschool football match in Chennai, Suraj's friends were at the juice shop, going over the game.
“The referee was blind,” said Rakesh. “Totally biased.”
Suraj had thought the referee was fair. The penalty was a real foul; he'd seen it clearly. But everyone was nodding.
“Totally biased,” he said.
Then Rakesh started imitating the way Rekha, the girl who scored the other team's goal, celebrated. Everyone laughed. Suraj thought her celebration had been brilliant. He laughed too, because the table was laughing.
On the way home, he felt tired, as though he'd carried something heavy. At the signal, a boy on a cycle did the same celebration, joyfully. Suraj smiled, a real smile this time, and felt a sting of shame about the juice shop.

qa.q: What did Rakesh say about the referee?
qa.a: He said the referee was blind and totally biased.

qa.q: Why did Suraj agree the referee was biased?
qa.a: He was afraid of standing apart from his friends, so their approval felt more important than what he had seen.

qa.q: What could Suraj try next time his friends mock someone?
qa.a: He could simply not laugh, or say he thought Rekha's celebration was great, keeping hold of his own view.

qa.q: How might Rekha feel if she knew the boys were mocking her celebration?
qa.a: Rekha would probably feel hurt and belittled after a moment she was proud of.

grounding: The passage shows a teenager agreeing with friends against his own view and laughing at mockery he dislikes because group approval feels more important.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, girls' hostel, 3rd year.
Nirmala is a kind, reliable student. I have noticed that she calls her mother before nearly every decision, even small ones: which elective, which kurta for the college fest, whether to join the NSS camp.
This week she was offered a summer research internship in Bengaluru. She was glowing when she told her roommate Sabina. Then she called home. Her parents want her in Madurai for the summer, as usual.
Afterward she sat in the common room a long time. Sabina told me she kept saying, “I'm a bad daughter for even wanting it.”
She loves her parents deeply; her own wishes are still finding room beside that love.
What I did next: I sat with her and told her that wanting something different is not the same as not loving her family. I have booked her a college counsellor appointment for Thursday, before she replies to the offer.

qa.q: Where was Nirmala offered a research internship?
qa.a: She was offered it in Bengaluru for the summer.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala keep saying she was a bad daughter?
qa.a: She felt guilty for having a wish that differed from her parents', torn between love for them and wanting the internship.

qa.q: What did the warden do that could help Nirmala?
qa.a: Reassured her that wanting something different isn't a lack of love, and booked a counsellor appointment so she can think it through.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel watching her roommate?
qa.a: Sabina probably feels worried and sympathetic, having seen Nirmala go from glowing to sad.

grounding: The warden's note shows a young woman from a close family seeking parental approval for every decision and feeling guilty when her wish differs.

passage:
Monday night.
I got the job offer from the Delhi publishing house. My first real one. I screamed into my pillow.
Then I did what I always do. I called Ma before I even told Bhavna. And Ma went quiet, then said, “Delhi is so far, beta. What about the job in Lucknow, near us?”
The Lucknow job is fine. But it isn't books.
Bhavna came in and saw my face. She said, “You want Delhi.” I said I didn't know. That's a lie. I do know. I just can't want it without feeling like I'm abandoning them.
I've asked Ma about everything, my stream, my college, my haircut. Her “good choice” has been my compass. Now it points one way and I point the other.
I love them. I also love this. I'm going to call Ma tomorrow and just tell her how much.
— Ganga

qa.q: Where is the publishing house that offered Ganga a job?
qa.a: The publishing house is in Delhi.

qa.q: Why can't Ganga want the Delhi job without feeling bad?
qa.a: Ganga feels guilty, as if choosing Delhi would mean abandoning the family, because Ma's approval has guided every decision.

qa.q: What is Ganga planning to do, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: Ganga plans to call Ma and honestly share how much the job matters, which respects both the love and Ganga's own wish.

qa.q: How might Ma feel when Ganga calls tomorrow?
qa.a: Ma might feel worried about the distance but also touched that Ganga is being honest with her.

grounding: The diary shows a young adult from a close family who seeks parental approval for every decision feeling guilty when a personal wish differs.

passage:
You asked what I noticed about Jomon, the guy who sat next to me at the agency. Okay.
I'm Jatin. Jomon said yes to everything. Extra slides for sales, yes. Covering someone's client call, yes. Weekend edits, yes. Everyone loved him. “Ask Jomon, he'll do it.”
By October he looked grey. He ate at his desk. Once I saw him close his eyes for a full minute during a meeting.
I felt uneasy, and honestly a bit guilty, because I'd asked him for things too.
So one day, when the manager asked him to take on a new pitch, I said, “Actually, I'll take half. Jomon's on the Kochi account.” He looked at me like I'd thrown him a rope.
Later I told him, “Next time you want to say no, say ‘let me check with Jatin.’ I'll back you.” He used it twice that month. Nobody thought less of him.

qa.q: What did Jatin say when the manager asked Jomon to take on a new pitch?
qa.a: Jatin said, “Actually, I'll take half. Jomon's on the Kochi account.”

qa.q: How did Jatin feel watching Jomon burn out?
qa.a: Jatin felt uneasy and a bit guilty, having also asked Jomon for things.

qa.q: What backup did Jatin offer, and why does it work?
qa.a: A phrase, “let me check with Jatin,” so Jomon could practise saying no without seeming unhelpful or losing standing.

qa.q: How did Jomon seem to feel when Jatin stepped in?
qa.a: Jomon seemed relieved and grateful, looking as if he'd been thrown a rope.

grounding: The spoken account shows a team member noticing a colleague who agrees to every request and burns out, and offering backup so he can say no.

passage:
I'm Yamini, and I've worked two desks down from Ujjwal for a year.
Everyone in the office knows Ujjwal never says no. Can you proofread this? Sure. Can you stay for the client call at nine? Sure. Can you do the Diwali decorations? Of course.
In November I started noticing things. He was the last to leave most nights. He'd stopped going to his Saturday football. His smile looked tight.
I don't know what he was feeling. But once, when our boss asked him to take a third project, I saw his hand grip the edge of his desk while he said, “No problem.”
That afternoon I stopped by. “If you ever want to say no, just tell them you're helping me on the audit. I'll confirm it.”
He laughed, embarrassed. Two days later, he actually used it. The boss just said, “Okay, fine.” Ujjwal looked amazed.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal stop going to on Saturdays?
qa.a: He stopped going to his Saturday football.

qa.q: What made Yamini decide to step in?
qa.a: Yamini felt concerned seeing Ujjwal grip the desk while saying “No problem,” sensing he was overwhelmed.

qa.q: Why did Yamini's offer help Ujjwal say no?
qa.a: It gave him a safe, credible reason to decline, so he could practise saying no without losing standing.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal react when the boss accepted his no?
qa.a: Ujjwal looked amazed and probably relieved that saying no didn't cost him anything.

grounding: The colleague's account shows a team member noticing a colleague who never says no and burns out, and offering backup so he can decline.

passage:
Monday: Rashmi watched Hansa say yes three times before lunch: an extra report, a colleague's shift, organising the office farewell. Hansa laughed, but her hands were shaking as she poured tea.
Thursday: Hansa was at her desk at 8 p.m. when Rashmi left. On Friday morning, Hansa had dark circles and had forgotten her own deadline. The manager frowned. Rashmi felt a pang of worry.
The next Monday: When a senior asked Hansa to cover yet another client meeting, Rashmi spoke first. “Hansa's with me on the vendor review this week. I can check if someone else is free.”
Later she whispered to Hansa, “You can say you're with me anytime. Practise.”
On Wednesday, Hansa said it herself. “I'm on the vendor review with Rashmi. Can we look at next week?” The senior nodded. Hansa sat back, stunned, and smiled.

qa.q: What three things did Hansa say yes to on Monday before lunch?
qa.a: An extra report, a colleague's shift, and organising the office farewell.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel when Hansa forgot her own deadline?
qa.a: Rashmi felt a pang of worry, seeing Hansa burning out quietly.

qa.q: What did Rashmi offer that let Hansa practise saying no?
qa.a: She offered a line, being “with Rashmi on the vendor review,” and backed it up so Hansa could decline without losing standing.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel when the senior nodded on Wednesday?
qa.a: Hansa felt stunned and relieved, surprised that saying no was accepted.

grounding: The three beats show a colleague noticing a teammate who agrees to everything and burns out, and offering backup so she can practise saying no.
